# Data
## First time
```{r import_and_cache_dia, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

# ============================================================
# 1. File paths and cache directory
# ============================================================

file_alpha <- "/Users/nvd448/Documents/MSProt2026/Search_outputs/AlphaDIA/precursor.matrix.tsv"

file_diann <- "/Users/nvd448/Documents/MSProt2026/Search_outputs/DIANN/Team2_DIA-NN_identification_results/Team2_DIA-NN_report.pr_matrix.tsv"

file_spectronaut <- "/Users/nvd448/Documents/MSProt2026/Search_outputs/Spectronaut/FilteredCleaned_Spectronaut_Report.RDS"

file_maxdia <- "/Users/nvd448/Documents/MSProt2026/Search_outputs/MaxQuant/Team4_MaxDIA_evidence.txt"

cache_dir <- "/Users/nvd448/Documents/MSProt2026/R_cache"

dir.create(cache_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

# ============================================================
# 2. AlphaDIA — preserve precursor hashes as character
# ============================================================

alpha_cache <- file.path(cache_dir, "alpha_raw_character_hash.rds")

if (file.exists(alpha_cache)) {

  alpha_raw <- readRDS(alpha_cache)

} else {

  alpha_raw <- readr::read_tsv(
    file_alpha,
    col_types = readr::cols(
      precursor.mod_seq_charge_hash = readr::col_character(),
      .default = readr::col_guess()
    ),
    show_col_types = FALSE
  )

  saveRDS(alpha_raw, alpha_cache, compress = FALSE)
}

# ============================================================
# 3. DIA-NN — original wide matrix
# ============================================================

diann_cache <- file.path(cache_dir, "diann_raw.rds")

if (file.exists(diann_cache)) {

  diann_raw <- readRDS(diann_cache)

} else {

  diann_raw <- readr::read_tsv(
    file_diann,
    show_col_types = FALSE
  )

  saveRDS(diann_raw, diann_cache, compress = FALSE)
}

# ============================================================
# 4. Spectronaut — already saved as RDS
# ============================================================

spectronaut_raw <- readRDS(file_spectronaut)

# ============================================================
# 5. MaxDIA — import essential columns with explicit types
# ============================================================

maxdia_cache <- file.path(cache_dir, "maxdia_selected_typed.rds")

if (file.exists(maxdia_cache)) {

  maxdia_raw <- readRDS(maxdia_cache)

} else {

  maxdia_header <- names(
    readr::read_tsv(
      file_maxdia,
      n_max = 0,
      show_col_types = FALSE
    )
  )

  keep_cols <- c(
    "Raw file",
    "Modified sequence",
    "Sequence",
    "Charge",
    "Leading proteins",
    "Proteins",
    "Intensity",
    "Q-value",
    "PEP",
    "Reverse",
    "Potential contaminant",
    "DIA evidence type"
  )

  missing_cols <- setdiff(keep_cols, maxdia_header)

  if (length(missing_cols) > 0) {
    stop(
      "Missing MaxDIA columns: ",
      paste(missing_cols, collapse = ", ")
    )
  }

  column_spec <- readr::cols(
    .default = readr::col_skip(),

    `Raw file` = readr::col_character(),
    `Modified sequence` = readr::col_character(),
    Sequence = readr::col_character(),
    Charge = readr::col_integer(),
    `Leading proteins` = readr::col_character(),
    Proteins = readr::col_character(),
    Intensity = readr::col_double(),
    `Q-value` = readr::col_double(),
    PEP = readr::col_double(),
    Reverse = readr::col_character(),
    `Potential contaminant` = readr::col_character(),
    `DIA evidence type` = readr::col_character()
  )

  maxdia_raw <- readr::read_tsv(
    file_maxdia,
    col_types = column_spec,
    show_col_types = FALSE
  )

  saveRDS(maxdia_raw, maxdia_cache, compress = FALSE)
}

# ============================================================
# 6. Verify imported datasets
# ============================================================

import_summary <- tibble(
  Software = c("AlphaDIA", "DIANN", "Spectronaut", "MaxDIA"),
  Rows = c(
    nrow(alpha_raw),
    nrow(diann_raw),
    nrow(spectronaut_raw),
    nrow(maxdia_raw)
  ),
  Columns = c(
    ncol(alpha_raw),
    ncol(diann_raw),
    ncol(spectronaut_raw),
    ncol(maxdia_raw)
  )
)

print(import_summary)

class(alpha_raw$precursor.mod_seq_charge_hash)
class(diann_raw$Precursor.Id)
class(spectronaut_raw$EG.PrecursorId)
class(maxdia_raw$`Modified sequence`)
```

```{r reload_cached_data}
# Reload all four datasets after an R crash

cache_dir <- "/Users/nvd448/Documents/MSProt2026/R_cache"

# Check that all required files exist
```

## Hemogenize datasets
```{r homogenize_datasets, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}

# ============================================================
# 1. AlphaDIA: wide -> long
# ============================================================

alpha_run_cols <- names(alpha_raw)[2:85]

alpha_long <- alpha_raw |>
  rename(
    Precursor.Id = precursor.mod_seq_charge_hash,
    Stripped.Sequence = precursor.sequence,
    Precursor.Charge = precursor.charge,
    Protein.Group = pg.name
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = all_of(alpha_run_cols),
    names_to = "Run",
    values_to = "Precursor.Quantity"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    Precursor.Id = as.character(Precursor.Id),
    Run = str_remove(
      basename(Run),
      regex("\\.raw$", ignore_case = TRUE)
    )
  )

# ============================================================
# 2. DIA-NN: wide -> long
# ============================================================

diann_run_cols <- names(diann_raw)[11:94]

diann_long <- diann_raw |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = all_of(diann_run_cols),
    names_to = "Run",
    values_to = "Precursor.Quantity"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    Precursor.Id = as.character(Precursor.Id),
    Run = str_remove(
      basename(Run),
      regex("\\.raw$", ignore_case = TRUE)
    )
  )

# ============================================================
# 3. Spectronaut: long -> standardized long
# ============================================================

spectronaut_long <- spectronaut_raw |>
  rename(
    Run = R.FileName,
    Precursor.Id = EG.PrecursorId,
    Stripped.Sequence = PEP.StrippedSequence,
    Protein.Group = PG.ProteinGroups,
    Precursor.Quantity = FG.Quantity,
    PEP = EG.PEP,
    Cscore = EG.Cscore,
    Decoy = EG.IsDecoy,
    IsImputed = EG.IsImputed
  ) |>
  mutate(
    Run = str_remove(
      basename(Run),
      regex("\\.raw$", ignore_case = TRUE)
    ),
    Precursor.Id = as.character(Precursor.Id)
  )

# ============================================================
# 4. MaxDIA: long -> standardized long
# ============================================================

maxdia_long <- maxdia_raw |>
  rename(
    Run = `Raw file`,
    Modified.Sequence = `Modified sequence`,
    Stripped.Sequence = Sequence,
    Precursor.Charge = Charge,
    Protein.Group = `Leading proteins`,
    Protein.Ids = Proteins,
    Precursor.Quantity = Intensity,
    Q.Value = `Q-value`,
    DIA.evidence.type = `DIA evidence type`
  ) |>
  mutate(
    Run = str_remove(
      basename(Run),
      regex("\\.raw$", ignore_case = TRUE)
    ),
    Precursor.Id = paste(
      Modified.Sequence,
      Precursor.Charge,
      sep = "_"
    )
  )

# ============================================================
# 5. Store standardized datasets in a list
# ============================================================

dia_long <- list(
  AlphaDIA = alpha_long,
  DIANN = diann_long,
  Spectronaut = spectronaut_long,
  MaxDIA = maxdia_long
)

# ============================================================
# 6. Check dimensions and number of runs
# ============================================================

format_summary <- purrr::imap_dfr(
  dia_long,
  function(dat, software) {
    tibble(
      Software = software,
      Rows = nrow(dat),
      Columns = ncol(dat),
      Runs = n_distinct(dat$Run)
    )
  }
)

print(format_summary)

```

Each row in the precursor data table is in “long format” and contains information about one precursor in a specific run.

```{r filter_precursors, message=FALSE}
# Spectronaut
spectronaut_filtered <- spectronaut_precursors |>
  filter(
    Decoy == FALSE,
    Potential.contaminant == "-",
    IsImputed == "False",
    !is.na(PEP),
    PEP <= 0.01,
    !is.na(Precursor.Quantity),
    Precursor.Quantity > 0

  arrange(Run, Precursor.Id, PEP, desc(Cscore)) |>
  distinct(Run, Precursor.Id, .keep_all = TRUE)

  filter(
    is.na(Reverse),
    is.na(Potential.contaminant),
    !is.na(Q.Value),

    !is.na(Precursor.Quantity),

  distinct(Run, Precursor.Id, .keep_all = TRUE)
```

```{r validate_filtered_precursors}

filtered_validation <- purrr::imap_dfr(
  precursors_filtered,
  function(dat, software) {

    dt <- data.table::as.data.table(
      dat[, c("Run", "Precursor.Id", "Precursor.Quantity")]
    )

    tibble(
      Software = software,
      Rows = nrow(dt),
      Runs = data.table::uniqueN(dt$Run),
      Missing_IDs = sum(is.na(dt$Precursor.Id)),
      Missing_Quantities = sum(is.na(dt$Precursor.Quantity)),
      Nonpositive_Quantities = sum(
        dt$Precursor.Quantity <= 0,
        na.rm = TRUE
      ),
      Duplicate_Keys = nrow(dt) -
        data.table::uniqueN(dt, by = c("Run", "Precursor.Id"))
    )
  }
)

print(filtered_validation)

```


The sample annotation table is not available and can be generated from the run labels, as the researchers included information on the design in the filenames.

```{r sample_annotation}
# ============================================================
# Generate sample annotations from run filenames
# ============================================================

make_annotation <- function(data) {

  tibble(
    runCol = unique(data$Run)
  ) |>
    mutate(
      # Standardize run names
      sampleId = basename(runCol),
      sampleId = str_remove(
        sampleId,
        regex("\\.(raw|mzML)$", ignore_case = TRUE)
      ),

      # Sample-set prefix (meaning to be confirmed)
      sample_set = str_extract(sampleId, "^Group[1-4]"),

      # Genotype
      genotype = case_when(
        str_detect(sampleId, regex("c-jun_KO", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "KO",
        str_detect(sampleId, regex("CTRL", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "CTRL",
        TRUE ~ NA_character_
      ),

      # Drug treatment
      treatment = case_when(
        str_detect(sampleId, regex("JNK-IN-8", ignore_case = TRUE)) &
          str_detect(sampleId, regex("cDDP", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "JNK_IN_8_cDDP",

        str_detect(sampleId, regex("JNK-IN-8", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "JNK_IN_8",

        str_detect(sampleId, regex("cDDP", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "cDDP",

        TRUE ~ "Untreated"
      ),

      # Treatment duration
      time = case_when(
        str_detect(sampleId, regex("06h", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "6h",
        str_detect(sampleId, regex("24h", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "24h",
        treatment == "Untreated" ~ "Baseline",
        TRUE ~ NA_character_
      ),

      # Final numeric suffix in the filename
      rep = str_extract(sampleId, "[0-9]+$"),

      # Combined experimental condition
      condition = case_when(
        !is.na(genotype) & !is.na(time) ~
          paste(genotype, treatment, time, sep = "_"),
        TRUE ~ NA_character_
      ),

      genotype = factor(genotype),
      treatment = factor(treatment),
      time = factor(time),
      condition = factor(condition),
      rep = factor(rep)
    ) |>
    arrange(sampleId)
}

# ============================================================
# Apply the function to all four datasets
# ============================================================

annot <- purrr::map(
  precursors,
  make_annotation
)

# ============================================================
# Inspect sample annotations
# ============================================================

# Number of runs per software
purrr::map_int(annot, nrow)

# Number of samples per experimental condition
purrr::map(
  annot,
  ~ count(.x, condition, name = "n_samples")
)

# Check whether any filenames could not be classified
purrr::map(
  annot,
  ~ filter(.x, is.na(genotype) | is.na(time))
)

# Verify that all software packages have identical sample IDs
identical_sample_ids <- all(
  purrr::map_lgl(
    annot,
    ~ identical(.x$sampleId, annot$DIANN$sampleId)
  )
)

cat("Identical sample IDs and order:", identical_sample_ids, "\n")

# Check missing annotation fields
purrr::imap_dfr(
  annot,
  ~ tibble(
    Software = .y,
    Missing_Genotype = sum(is.na(.x$genotype)),
    Missing_Treatment = sum(is.na(.x$treatment)),
    Missing_Time = sum(is.na(.x$time)),
    Missing_Condition = sum(is.na(.x$condition)),
    Duplicate_Sample_IDs = sum(duplicated(.x$sampleId))
  )
)
```
## Qfeatures
Here, Precursor.Quantity provides the quantitative values, and Precursor.Id identifies the precursor features.

```{r create_qfeatures, message=FALSE}
# ============================================================
# Create one QFeatures object per software
# ============================================================

qf <- purrr::imap(
  precursors_filtered,
  function(dat, software) {

    readQFeatures(
      assayData = dat,
      colData = annot[[software]],
      quantCols = "Precursor.Quantity",
      runCol = "Run",
      fnames = "Precursor.Id"
    )
  }
)

# Inspect each QFeatures object
purrr::map(qf, assayNames)

# Inspect dimensions
purrr::map(
  qf,
  ~ lapply(assayNames(.x), function(nm) dim(.x[[nm]]))
)
```


# Data preprocessing
The data preprocessing workflow for DIA data is similar to the workflow for DDA-LFQ data, but there are suble differences as we start from precursor level data and have additional columns. 

## Missing values
The first preprocessing step is to correctly encode the missing values. It is important that missing values are encoded using `NA`. For instance, non-observed values should not be encoded with a zero because true zeros (the proteomic feature is absent from the sample) cannot be distinguished from technical zeros (the feature was missed by the instrument or could not be identified). We therefore replace any zero in the quantitative data with an `NA`.

```{r}
qf <- zeroIsNA(qf, names(qf))
```
Note that `msqrob2` can handle missing data without having to rely on hard-to-verify imputation assumptions, which is our general recommendation. However, `msqrob2` does not prevent users from using imputation, which can be performed with `impute() `from the `QFeatures` package.

## Filtering
Filtering removes low-quality and unreliable precursors that would otherwise introduce noise and artefacts in the data. We apply standard filtering advised by DIA-NN:

1. q-value threshold of 0.01 for the identification of precursors (Q.Value) and protein groups (PG.Q.Value). If the file is processed via matching between runs, it is also useful to filter on Lib.Q.Value and Lib.PG.Q.Value.

2. Remove precursors that could not be mapped, i.e. when Precursor.Id column is an empty string.

3. Filter decoys, i.e. only keep precursors for which the Decoy column equals 0. (Note, that the Decoy column is not present in the output of older versions of DIA-NN)

4. Keeping only proteotypic peptides, which map uniquely to a specific protein.
```{r}
qf <-  qf |>
  filterFeatures(~ Q.Value <= 0.01 & #1.
                     PG.Q.Value <= 0.01 &  #1.
                     Lib.Q.Value <= 0.01 & #1.
                     Lib.PG.Q.Value <= 0.01 & #1.
                     Precursor.Id != "" & #2.
                     Decoy == 0 & #3. (Note, that this filter is not available with previous versions of DIA-NN, as the report.tsv file did not include a Decoy column. So other strategies are needed if Decoys are in the output file.)
                     Proteotypic == 1) #4.
```
Note, that it is important that the filtering criteria are not distorting the distribution of the test statistics in the downstream analysis for features that are non-DA.

(Assay joining, an extra step compare to previous DDA workflow)

Up to now, the data from different runs were kept in separate assays. We can now join the normalised sets into an precursor set using joinAssays(). Sets are joined by stacking the columns (samples) in a matrix and rows (features) are matched according to a row identifier, here the `Precursor.Id`. We will store the result in the assay with name: `precursor`.
```{r}
(qf <- joinAssays(
  x = qf,
  i = names(qf),
  fcol = "Precursor.Id",
  name = "precursors"
  ))
```
```{r}
qf[,,"precursors"] |> 
  longForm(colvars = colnames(colData(qf))) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = sampleId)) +
  geom_bar(aes(fill = factor(!is.na(value))),
           colour = "black") +
  theme_minimal()
```

We keep peptides that were observed at last 4 times out of the 9 samples, so 
that we can estimate the peptide characteristics, so we keep peptides that are 
observed in at least 44.4% of the samples, which corresponds to one treatment 
condition. This is an arbitrary value that may need to be adjusted depending on
the experiment and the data set.
```{r}
nObs <- 4
n <- ncol(qf[["precursors"]])

(qf <- filterNA(qf, i = "precursors", pNA = (n - nObs) / n))
```
Here, we remove proteins that can only be found by one peptide, as such proteins may not be trustworthy.

1. We first calculate how many distinct peptides map to each protein (Protein.Group). We use the stripped precursor sequence, i.e. sequence of the base peptide for this purpose.

2. We store this information in the row data of the precursors assay

3. We filter precursors of one-hit wonder proteins.
```{r}
# Filter for peptides per protein
pepsPerProtDf <- qf[["precursors"]] |> 
    rowData() |> 
    data.frame() |>
    dplyr::select("Stripped.Sequence", "Protein.Group") |>
    group_by(Protein.Group) |>
    mutate(pepsPerProt = Stripped.Sequence |>
               unique() |> length()
           ) #1.

rowData(qf[["precursors"]])$pepsPerProt <- pepsPerProtDf$pepsPerProt #2. 

qf <- filterFeatures(qf, 
                              ~ pepsPerProt > 1, 
                              keep = TRUE) #3.
```
## Log-transformation
For this, we perform a short data manipulation pipeline:

1. We use `longForm()` to convert the QFeatures object into a long table, where each row contains the quantitative information about one observation, in which column, row and set it was found. Long tables are particularly useful for manipulating data with the tidyverse ecosystem, namely with ggplot2 for visualisation. `longForm()` also allows to include annotations, and we here include `Mixture` and `TechRepMixture` for filtering and colouring.
2. `longForm()` returns a `DataFrame` which we convert to a `data.frame`.
3. We filter the data to keep only the data from precursor “(UniMod:1)ADSRDPASDQMQHWK3”.
```{r}
dat <- longForm(qf, colvars = colnames(colData(qf))) |> ## 1.
  data.frame() |> ## 2.
  filter(rowname == "(UniMod:1)ADSRDPASDQMQHWK3") ## 3.

# Left plot: original scale
p1 <- ggplot(dat, aes(x = ratio, y = value)) +
  geom_point(color = "black", size = 2) +
  labs(
    x = "ratio",
    y = "value"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

# Right plot: log2 scale
p2 <- ggplot(dat, aes(x = log2(ratio), y = log2(value))) +
  geom_point(color = "black", size = 2) +
  labs(
    x = "UPS ratio (left original, right (log2))",
    y = "log2(value)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

# Combine plots
(p1 | p2) +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "UPS precursor ADSRDPASDQMQHWK3"
  )
```
Upon, log2-transformation we can see that the problem of unequal variability is solved. Another advantages of log2-transformation is that it provides a scale that directly relates to biological interpretation. We perform log2-transformation with `logTransform()` from the `QFeatures` package. We use `base = 2` and store the result in a new summarized experiment named `precursors_log`.
```{r}
qf <- logTransform(qf, 
                      base = 2, 
                      i = "precursors", 
                      name = "precursors_log")
```

## Normalization
The most common objective of MS-based proteomics experiments is to understand the biological changes in protein abundance between experimental conditions. However, changes in measurements between groups can be caused due to technical factors. For instance, there are systematic fluctuations from run-to-run that shift the measured intensity distribution. We can this explore as follows:

1. We extract the sets containing the log transformed data. This is performed using `QFeatures`’ 3-way subsetting.
2. We use `longForm()` to convert the `QFeatures` object into a long table, including `condition` and concentration for filtering and coloring.
3. We visualize the density of the quantitative values within each sample. We color each sample based on its spike-in condition.

```{r}
qf[, , "precursors_log"] |> #1.
  longForm(colvars = colnames(colData(qf))) |>  #2. 
  data.frame() |> 
  filter(!is.na(value)) |>
  ggplot() + #3.
  aes(x = value,
      colour = condition,
      group = colname) +
  geom_density() +
  theme_minimal()
```
Even in this clean synthetic data set (same yeast background with some spiked UPS proteins), the marginal precursor intensity distributions across samples are not well aligned. Ignoring this effect will increase the noise and reduce the statistical power of the experiment, and may also, in case of unbalanced designs, introduce confounding effects that will bias the results. Here, we will use the Median of Ratios method of DESeq2, which was originally developed for RNA-seq data analysis and can also correct for differences in composition of the proteomes in the different samples.

1. We calculate the log transformed normalisation factor from the Median of Ratios method
2. Subtract these log2-norm factors from the intensities of each corresponding column of the assay data and store the result in the new assay peptides_norm.
```{r}
nfLog <- nfLogMedianOfRatios(qf, "precursors_log") #1.

qf<- sweep( #Subtract log2 norm factor column-by-column (MARGIN = 2) #2.
  qf,
  MARGIN = 2,
  STATS = nfLog,
  i = "precursors_log",
  name = "precursors_norm"
)

```
Note that users can also use all normalisation functions that are provided in QFeatures, i.e. by replacing the sweep function by `QFeatures::normalize` or that they can start from intensities normalised by DIA-NN, e.g. `Precursor.Normalised`.

```{r}
qf[, , "precursors_norm"] |>
  longForm(colvars = colnames(colData(qf))) |> 
  data.frame() |> 
  filter(!is.na(value)) |>
  ggplot() + 
  aes(x = value,
      colour = condition,
      group = colname) +
  geom_density() +
  labs(subtitle = "Normalised log2 precursor intensities") +
  theme_minimal()
```
Upon normalisation, we can see that the distributions nicely overlap.

## Aggregation
The objective of aggregation is to summarise the precursor-level intensities into a protein expression value. We illustrate the motivation for summarisation using all peptide-level data for one of the spiked UPS proteins. 
```{r}
protName <- "UPS|P01008ups|ANT3_HUMAN_UPS"
qf[,,"precursors_norm"] |> 
  longForm(colvars = colnames(colData(qf)), rowvars = "Protein.Ids") |> 
  data.frame() |> 
  filter(Protein.Ids == protName) |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x = rowname, 
      y = value,
      group = colname) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.1) +
  geom_point(aes(fill = condition), size = 3, shape = 21) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 1, vjus = 0.5),
        legend.position = "top") + 
  labs(
       subtitle = protName,
       x = "Precursor", 
       y = "log2(norm Intensity)") +
  theme_minimal()+
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 1))
```

1. We can see that data for a protein can consist of many precursors, hence the need for summarisation.
2. We observe that different precursors have different intensities within the same sample (same line). This is because different precursors have different properties and hence differ in their ionisation efficiency, which will influence the detectability in the MS (Challenges).
3. The precursor identification are inconsistent between groups of interest. We can see the low-concentration group (condition a, red) display more missing values than the high-concentration group (condition e, blue). Moreover, which value is missing depends on the precursor characteristics. All the precursors found in the low-concentration group are the most intense precursors in the high concentration group.
4. We also often find outliers, for instance, due to misidentification or fluctuations during MS acquisition.
5. These data also suggest pseudo-replication. The precursor intensities in one same sample (dots connected by a line) are correlated, i.e. they more alike than the precursor intensities between samples (the lines do not perfectly align).

The fact that different precursors have different intensities (2.), may be inconsistently identified (3.) and/or quantified (4.), and show sample correlations (5.) can lead to bias if we use simple summarisation approaches such as summing or averaging the precursor intensities for each sample. Instead, we will resort to more advanced summarisation approaches to accommodate for these issues. Here, we summarise the precursor-level data into protein intensities usin`g maxLFQ`. It is implemented in the `maxLFQ` function of the `iq` package.
```{r}
(qf <- aggregateFeatures(
  qf, i = "precursors_norm", 
  name = "proteins",
  fcol = "Protein.Group", 
#  fun = MsCoreUtils::medianPolish,
#  na.rm = TRUE
  fun = function(X, ...) iq::maxLFQ(X)$estimate
))

qf["UPS|P01008ups|ANT3_HUMAN_UPS", , ]
```
```{r}
qf[, , "proteins"] |>
  longForm(colvars = colnames(colData(qf))) |> 
  data.frame() |> 
  filter(!is.na(value)) |>
  ggplot() + 
  aes(x = value,
      colour = condition,
      group = colname) +
  geom_density() +
  theme_minimal() +
   labs(subtitle = "Normalised log2 protein intensities")
plot(qf)
```

The data processing is complete.

# Data modeling
Each sample has been synthetically created to contain a constant yeast 
background where human lysates were spiked in at five different concentration. 
Each sample preparation has been replicated three times. So, the key question is
“can our model retrieve the proteins that have been spiked in across the 
conditions?” Moreover, since we know the expected protein abundance in each 
sample, we will also be able to assess how accurate the model can estimate the 
average fold changes between spike-in conditions.

In this experimental design, we can model a single source of variation: 
spike-in concentration. 
All remaining sources of variability, e.g. pipetting errors, MS run to run 
variability, etc will be lumped in the residual variability (error term).

Spike-in condition effects: we model the source of variation induced by the 
experimental treatment of interest as a fixed effect, which we consider 
non-random, i.e. the treatment effect is assumed to be the same in repeated 
experiments, but it is unknown and has to be estimated.

When modelling a typical label-free experiment at the protein level, the model 
boils down to the following linear model: 
$y_i = \mathbf{x}_i^T \boldsymbol{\beta} + \epsilon_i$.

with $y_i$ the$log_2$-normalised and summarised protein intensities in sample 
$i$; $x_i$ a vector with the covariate pattern for the sample encoding the 
intercept, spike-in condition, or other experimental factors; 
$\boldsymbol{\beta}$ the vector of parameters that model the association between
the covariates and the outcome; and $\epsilon_i$ the residuals reflecting 
variation that is not captured by the fixed effects. 
In R, this model is encoded using the following simple formula:
```{r}
model <- ~ condition
```

We estimate the model with `msqrob()`. The function takes the `QFeatures` 
object, extracts the quantitative values from the `"proteins"` set generated 
during summarisation, and fits a simple linear model with `condition` as 
covariate, which are automatically retrieved from `colData(qf)`.

```{r setup, include=TRUE, echo=TRUE, eval=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE }
qf <- msqrob(
  qf,  i = "proteins",
  formula = model,
  robust = TRUE # improving robustness against outliers
)
```
The fitting results are available in the `msqrobModels` column of the `rowData`.
More specifically, the modelling output is stored in the `rowData` as a
`statModel` object, one model per row (protein).
```{r}
models <- rowData(qf[["proteins"]])[["msqrobModels"]]
models[1:3]
```
## Statistical inference
We can now convert the research question “do the spike-in conditions affect the protein intensities?” into a statistical hypothesis. In other words, we need to translate this question in a null and alternative hypothesis on a single model parameter or a linear combination of model parameters, which is also referred to with a contrast.
```{r}
vd <- ExploreModelMatrix::VisualizeDesign(
    sampleData =  colData(qf),
    designFormula = model,
    textSizeFitted = 4
)
vd$plotlist
```
This plot shows that the average protein $log_2$ intensity for `condition2` 
is modelled by `(Intercept)`, for the `condition4` group by 
`(Intercept) + condtion4` and for the `condition8` group by 
`(Intercept) + condtion8`. Hence, to assess differential abundance of proteins 
between spike-in conditions, we will have to assess all pairwise combinations 
between the spike-in groups, which leads to 3 different contrasts.

This combination of parameters is also called a contrast. Thus, we assess the 
following null hypothesis for this contrast: `condition4 = 0` with our 
statistical test.
`makeContrast()` converts the hypothesis into a formal contrast matrix with 
parameter names as rows and hypotheses in columns. 

```{r}
contrast <- "condition4 = 0"
(L <- makeContrast(
  contrast,
   parameterNames = colnames(vd$designmatrix)
))
```

We can now test our null hypothesis using `hypothesisTest()` which takes the 
`QFeatures` object with the fitted model and the contrast we just built. 
`msqrob2` automatically applies the hypothesis testing to all proteins in 
the data.
```{r}
qf <- hypothesisTest(qf, i = "proteins", contrast = L)
```
The results are stored in the set containing the model, here `proteins`. We 
retrieve the results from the `rowData`. Note, that for this spike-in study we 
know the ground truth, so we also add variable `isUPS` to indicate if the 
protein is spiked (UPS). There is also easier to use the novel getter function 
from msqrob2 `msqrobCollect`.
```{r}
inference <- rowData(qf[["proteins"]])$condition4 
head(inference)

inference <- msqrobCollect(qf[["proteins"]], L)
head(inference)
```

```{r}
alpha <- 0.05 
volcano <- plotVolcano(inference,significanceLevel = alpha) + 
  labs(subtitle = paste0(colnames(L), " = 0"))
volcano 

signif <- inference |>
  filter(adjPval < alpha) |>
  arrange(pval)
knitr::kable(signif)
```
Note, that we return many true positives and one false positive.

We can explore the quantitative data of the significant proteins using a heatmap. 
1. we select the names of the proteins that were declared significant 
between condition A and condition B and extract their quantitative data. 
2. We extract the quantitative data and scale by rows with `assay()`. 
3. We will create a heatmap using the `ComplexHeatmap` package, which enables 
heatmap annotations. We will annotate the heatmap using our model
variables `condition` and `lab`.
4. We now make the heatmap.
```{r}
sig <- inference |> 
  filter(adjPval < alpha) |> 
  arrange(pval) |> 
  pull(feature) #1.

se <- getWithColData(qf, "proteins")
quants <- t(scale(t(assay(se[sig,])))) #2. 

colnames(quants) <- paste0("con", se$condition,"_rep",se$rep) #specific to this dataset to get short colnames
annotations <- columnAnnotation(
  condition = se$condition
) #3.

set.seed(1234) ## annotation colours are randomly generated by default
heatmap <- Heatmap(
                       quants, 
                       name = "log2 intensity",
                       top_annotation = annotations, 
                       column_title = contrast
                       ) #4.
heatmap
```
## All contrasts
With the createPairwiseContrast function we can make all pairwise contrasts for a model.

```{r}
(allHypotheses <- createPairwiseContrasts(
  model, colData(qf), "condition"
  )
)

(L <- makeContrast(
  allHypotheses,
  parameterNames = colnames(vd$designmatrix)
))
```
```{r}
qf <- hypothesisTest(qf, 
                              i = "proteins", 
                              contrast = L,
                              overwrite = TRUE)
```

List with significant deferentially abundant proteins:
```{r}
inferences <- msqrobCollect(qf[["proteins"]], L)

for (j in colnames(L)) #3. 
{
  inference <- inferences |> filter(adjPval < alpha & contrast == j)
  cat("**Contrast:**", j, "= 0 (", nrow(inference |> filter(adjPval < alpha)), "significant proteins)\n\n") #8.
  print(kable(inference |> arrange(pval) |> relocate("feature"), row.names = FALSE)) #9.
  cat("\n\n\n---\n\n") #10.
}

volcanoplots <- inferences |> 
  plotVolcano() +
  facet_wrap(~contrast)
volcanoplots
```
We conduct heatmaps for the significant metabolites for each contrast.

We first extract the normalised assay metabolites_norm along with its colData.
We make an empty list heatmaps to store the plots.
We will loop over the column names of the contrast matrix L
We extract the names of the significant features for contrast i
We extract the quant data for the significant metabolites
We extract annotation
We make the heatmap using the quants data. We do not cluster columns (samples) to keep them together according to the design.
```{r}

heatmaps <- lapply(colnames(L),
                   function(contrast, se, alpha)
                   {
                     sig <- rowData(se)[[contrast]] |> 
                       filter(adjPval < alpha) |> 
                       rownames()
                     quants <- t(scale(t(assay(se[sig,]))))
                     colnames(quants) <- paste0("con", se$condition,"_rep",se$rep)
                     annotations <- columnAnnotation(condition = se$condition)
                     set.seed(1234) ## annotation colours are randomly generated by default
                     return(
                       Heatmap(
                       quants, 
                       name = "log2 intensity",
                       top_annotation = annotations, 
                       column_title = paste0(contrast, " = 0")
                       )
                     )
                   },
                   se = getWithColData(qf, "proteins"),
                   alpha = alpha)

heatmaps
```
## Precursor-level analysis:
525 UPS2 precursor entries rather than all 34,421
```{r, warning=FALSE}
model_prec <- ~ condition

# Extract UPS2 precursor indices
ups_idx <- which(
  rowData(qf[["precursors_norm"]])$species == "ups"
)

# Create a separate QFeatures object
qf_ups <- qf

# Keep only UPS2 precursor entries in the target assay
qf_ups[["precursors_norm"]] <-
  qf_ups[["precursors_norm"]][ups_idx, ]

# Fit robust models
qf_ups <- msqrob(
  qf_ups,
  i = "precursors_norm",
  formula = model_prec,
  robust = TRUE
)

# Inspect results
# 1. Check the model coefficient names
colnames(model.matrix(~ condition, data = as.data.frame(colData(qf_ups))))

# 2. Define the contrast: ratio04 vs ratio02
# 1. Define all three contrasts
L_ups <- makeContrast(
  c(
    "condition4 = 0",               # ratio04 vs ratio02
    "condition8 = 0",               # ratio08 vs ratio02
    "condition8 - condition4 = 0"   # ratio08 vs ratio04
  ),
  parameterNames = colnames(
    model.matrix(~ condition, data = as.data.frame(colData(qf_ups)))
  )
)

# 2. Test all three contrasts
qf_ups <- hypothesisTest(
  qf_ups,
  i = "precursors_norm",
  contrast = L_ups
)

# 3. Collect results for each contrast separately
inference_ups_04_02 <- msqrobCollect(
  qf_ups[["precursors_norm"]], L_ups[, 1, drop = FALSE]
)

inference_ups_08_02 <- msqrobCollect(
  qf_ups[["precursors_norm"]], L_ups[, 2, drop = FALSE]
)

inference_ups_08_04 <- msqrobCollect(
  qf_ups[["precursors_norm"]], L_ups[, 3, drop = FALSE]
)

# 4. Inspect results
head(inference_ups_04_02)
head(inference_ups_08_02)
head(inference_ups_08_04)

# 5. Create volcano plots
alpha_ups <- 0.05

# Create the three plots
p1 <- plotVolcano(inference_ups_04_02, significanceLevel = alpha_ups) +
  labs(title = "ratio04 vs ratio02")

p2 <- plotVolcano(inference_ups_08_02, significanceLevel = alpha_ups) +
  labs(title = "ratio08 vs ratio02")

p3 <- plotVolcano(inference_ups_08_04, significanceLevel = alpha_ups) +
  labs(title = "ratio08 vs ratio04")

# Find common axis limits from the plotted data
plots <- list(p1, p2, p3)

ranges <- lapply(plots, function(p) {
  b <- ggplot_build(p)
  data.frame(
    x = unlist(lapply(b$data, function(d) d$x)),
    y = unlist(lapply(b$data, function(d) d$y))
  )
})

all_xy <- do.call(rbind, ranges)

x_lim <- range(all_xy$x, finite = TRUE)
y_lim <- c(0, max(all_xy$y, na.rm = TRUE))

# Apply identical scales without dropping observations
common_scale <- list(
  coord_cartesian(xlim = x_lim, ylim = y_lim)
)

(p1 + common_scale | p2 + common_scale | p3 + common_scale) +
  plot_layout(ncol = 3)
```
